title: Database Scaling Techniques
description: Learn read replicas, write scaling, partitioning, and sharding strategies for scaling databases in production systems.

data.text: Databases are often the hardest component to scale because they manage durable, consistent state. As traffic grows, you need strategies that preserve data integrity while increasing throughput and availability.
Upgrading the database server—more CPU, RAM, or faster storage—is the simplest first step. It works well in the early stages, but costs rise quickly and hardware ceilings limit long-term growth.

Read replicas are copies of a primary database that handle read traffic. Writes still go to the primary, which asynchronously replicates changes to replicas. This pattern dramatically increases read capacity without changing application logic.

items: Offloads read-heavy workloads from the primary
Replicas can be placed closer to users for lower latency
Not a solution for write bottlenecks

data.text: Sharding splits data across multiple databases by a shard key, such as user ID or geographic region. Each shard holds a subset of the data, turning one large database into many smaller, manageable ones.

data.title: Caution
data.text: Sharding introduces cross-shard queries, rebalancing complexity, and operational overhead. Treat it as a last resort after exhausting vertical scaling and read replicas.

data.caption: Primary database with read replicas and sharded data stores
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    App[Application] --> Writer[Primary Writer]
    Writer -->|replication| Rep1[Read Replica 1]
    Writer -->|replication| Rep2[Read Replica 2]
    App -->|reads| Rep1 & Rep2
    App -->|shard by region| ShardA[Shard: NA]
    App -->|shard by region| ShardB[Shard: EU]
    App -->|shard by region| ShardC[Shard: APAC]
    ShardA & ShardB & ShardC --> Data[(Data)]

data.text: Writes are harder to scale than reads because they require synchronization. Strategies include write partitioning by key, using message queues to absorb bursts, or adopting multi-master or consensus-based databases when global writes are unavoidable.

data.title: Summary
points: Start with vertical scaling and read replicas before sharding.
Sharding solves scale but adds significant complexity.
Match the shard key to your most common access patterns.
Monitor replication lag and cross-shard query cost continuously.
data.takeaway: Database scaling is a ladder, not a switch. Climb it deliberately.

items.question: When should I introduce read replicas?
items.answer: When read throughput consistently approaches 70-80% of the primary's capacity, or when read latency affects user experience.

items.question: Is sharding always the final step?
items.answer: Often yes, but consider managed distributed databases or caching layers before manually sharding. Manual sharding should be a deliberate choice with clear boundaries.
